To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the evidence for cognitive interventions that are effective in improving cognitive abilities in older adults is not yet conclusive, that the transfer of intervention effects is not yet well understood and requires further research, and that the concept of plastic change in old age needs to be refined to account for the heterogeneity in the aging brain.
cognitive intervention research has not yet produced evidence that cognitive training can enhance cognitive performance across the board.

(1) cognitive plasticity is a fundamental characteristic of human brain function that is maintained in adulthood and old, (2) the plasticity of cognitive performance is not uniform across all cognitive abilities and (3) the plasticity potential of cognitive abilities declines with age.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question whether the plastic potential of the aging brain can be tapped by training interventions.
the question of whether cognitive interventions can be effective in enhancing the performance of older adults in tasks that are not explicitly practiced during the course of training.
the generality of intervention effects in the context of the plasticity of cognitive abilities in adulthood and old-age.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of cognitive training on the general level of cognitive abilities are not robust and that the effects on the level of specific abilities are not yet well understood.
the evidence for cognitive plasticity is inconclusive.

the effects of cognitive interventions on cognitive abilities in older adults are small and restricted to the trained domain, and that there is a need for a better understanding of the mechanisms that determine the scope of cognitive intervention effects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, despite the impressive evidence for the potential of cognitive interventions, the field has yet to demonstrate the existence of a generalizable cognitive plasticity in old age.
the evidence base for cognitive interventions that enable older adults to fulfill their cognitive plastic potential is still in its infancy.
the potential for cognitive intervention to improve everyday competence in old people is not fully understood.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the generality of intervention effects has been insufficiently investigated, and that future intervention studies should adopt a more comprehensive approach.
cognitive intervention studies should not be considered successful if they do not demonstrate generalizable effects on cognitive abilities and skills.
